title: Game Theory
subtitle: Strategy, equilibrium, cooperation and auctions, with runnable Python labs and live simulations
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A hands-on introduction to game theory: players, strategies and payoffs; dominance and Nash equilibrium; mixed strategies and the minimax theorem; the classic games of dilemma, trust, chicken and coordination; sequential games with backward induction and credible threats; repeated games and the evolution of cooperation; evolutionary game theory with replicator dynamics; auctions, bargaining and mechanism design; and cooperative games with the Shapley value and social choice with Arrow's theorem. Every chapter has Python labs verified in the built-in interpreter, a tournament of repeated-game strategies and a replicator dynamics lab.

chapters.title: Games, players and payoffs

maps.title: Basics
links: Normal form | is | A payoff matrix
Common knowledge | is | Known by all

summary: Game theory studies strategic situations where each person's best choice depends on what the others choose. A game lists the players, the strategies each can pick, and the payoff each gets for every combination.
A two-player game with few strategies is shown as a payoff matrix: rows for one player, columns for the other, and each cell holds a pair of payoffs.

Players are assumed rational: they pick strategies to maximise their own utility, and they know the others do the same. Games can be simultaneous or sequential, one-shot or repeated, competitive or cooperative.

glossary.def: A model of strategic interaction: players, strategies and payoffs.
A complete plan of action for a player.
The number a player receives for an outcome, expressing how much they like it.
A game described by a matrix of payoffs for every combination of strategies.
A game in which one player's gain is exactly the other's loss.

keyPoints: Players, strategies, payoffs.
Cell (row, column) = (payoff of row, payoff of column).
Rationality: maximise your own payoff.
Payoff numbers express preference, not money alone.
Zero-sum: payoffs add to a constant.

items: ELI5. A game is anything where what is best for you depends on what the other person does, like deciding whether to share a toy or grab it.

Two shopkeepers on the same street must each decide whether to cut prices. If both cut, profits fall. If only one cuts, that shop takes the customers. If neither cuts, both do fine. Each shopkeeper's best move depends on the other's choice. That is a game.

To write a game down, list three things. The players. For each player, the strategies available. And the payoffs: for every combination of strategies, a number for each player saying how good the result is for them.
The payoff numbers are utilities, which capture preferences, including risk and values, not only money.

For two players with a few strategies, the payoffs go in a matrix. The row player chooses a row, the column player chooses a column, and the cell shows two numbers, first the row player's payoff and then the column player's. Reading the matrix is the first skill of the subject.

Some games are purely competitive. In a zero-sum game, such as poker without the house cut, one player's gain is exactly the other's loss. Most real situations are mixed: there are gains from cooperation and also conflicts, and understanding the tension between them is the heart of the matter.

The assumptions matter. We say players are rational, meaning each tries to get the highest payoff, and that rationality is common knowledge: I know you are rational, you know that I know, and so on. Later chapters relax this, with evolution and learning, but we begin with the clean case.

options: One player's gain equals the other's loss

quiz.q: What does rational mean here?

practice.intro: Pair each term with its meaning.

practice.title: Read a cell
practice.intro: Write payoffs(game, r, c): the pair of payoffs [row payoff, column payoff] at row index r and column index c of a game given as a list of rows of [a, b] pairs.
practice.hint: Index the row then the column.

practice.title: Is it zero-sum?
practice.intro: Write zero_sum(game): True if every cell's two payoffs add to the same constant (the sum is the same in all cells), otherwise False.
practice.hint: Compare each cell's sum with the first.

practice.title: Expected payoff
practice.intro: Write expected(payoffs, probs): the expected value of a list of payoffs under a list of probabilities, rounded to 4 decimals.
practice.hint: Multiply and add.

practice.title: Best response
practice.intro: Write best_response(game, col): the row index with the highest row payoff when the column player plays column index col. If several rows tie return the smallest index.
practice.hint: Compare the first payoff in each row of that column.

chapters.title: Dominance and Nash equilibrium

maps.title: Equilibrium
links: Nash equilibrium | is | Mutual best replies

summary: A strategy strictly dominates another if it gives a higher payoff whatever the opponent does. A rational player never plays a dominated strategy, and removing dominated strategies can simplify a game, sometimes solving it.

A best response is the strategy that maximises your payoff given what the others do. A Nash equilibrium is a combination of strategies where each player's strategy is a best response to the others, so no one gains by changing alone.
To find pure Nash equilibria in a matrix, check every cell: is the row payoff the best in its column, and the column payoff the best in its row?

glossary.def: A strategy that is at least as good as all alternatives whatever the others do, and better in some case.
The strategy that maximises a player's payoff given the others' choices.
A profile of strategies in which each is a best response to the others.
A strategy chosen with certainty, without randomisation.
Repeatedly deleting strictly dominated strategies.

keyPoints: Nash: no one can gain by switching alone.
Check each cell: row best in column and column best in row.
Dominated strategies are never Nash strategies.
A game may have none, one or several pure equilibria.
Nash proved mixed equilibria always exist.

items: ELI5. A choice is steady when nobody wants to change their own move once they see everyone else's. That steady spot is called an equilibrium.

Two drivers approach a narrow bridge from opposite ends. If both stay, they crash. If one yields, the other passes. The question is what happens if each assumes the other is also thinking carefully. We need a solution concept, a rule that picks out the sensible outcomes of a game.
The most famous is the Nash equilibrium.

Start with the easy case, dominance. If one of my strategies pays more than another whatever you do, I would never play the lower one. Remove it. Then check whether your strategies have become dominated in the smaller game. Repeat.
If the process leaves one cell, the game is solved by iterated elimination.

Often nothing is dominated, so we use the best response idea. Given what you do, what is my best reply? A Nash equilibrium is a cell where my strategy is a best reply to yours and yours is a best reply to mine. Neither of us can do better by changing our own choice, so the outcome is stable.

To find the equilibria in a matrix, mark with a star the best payoff for the row player in each column, and the best payoff for the column player in each row. Any cell where both payoffs are starred is a pure Nash equilibrium. Some games have none, some have exactly one, and some have several.
John Nash proved in 1950 that every finite game has at least one equilibrium if mixed strategies are allowed, which the next chapter explains. He won the Nobel Prize in 1994 for it.
A stable outcome is not the same as a good one: in the prisoner's dilemma, the unique equilibrium is worse for both than another outcome.

quiz.q: What is a dominated strategy?
options: One that is worse whatever the opponent does

quiz.q: What is a Nash equilibrium?
options: Everyone is best-responding to the others

quiz.q: How can you find pure equilibria in a matrix?
options: Mark best replies and find cells with both marked

quiz.q: Is a Nash equilibrium always efficient?
What did Nash prove?
options: Every finite game has an equilibrium in mixed strategies

quiz.q: Can a game have several equilibria?

practice.intro: Pair each term with its meaning.

practice.title: Pure Nash equilibria
practice.intro: Write nash(game): all cells (r, c) of a two-player game (list of rows of [a, b] pairs) where the row payoff is the maximum in its column and the column payoff is the maximum in its row (ties count as best). Return the list of [r, c] pairs sorted.
practice.hint: Check all rows in the column and all columns in the row.

practice.title: Row dominant strategy
practice.intro: Write row_dominant(game): the index of a row that strictly dominates all other rows (payoff greater in every column against every other row), or -1 if there is none.
practice.hint: Compare row r with every other row in every column.

practice.title: Eliminate dominated rows
practice.intro: Write eliminate_rows(game): repeatedly delete any row strictly dominated by another row (all of its row payoffs are lower in every column), considering only rows. Return the list of remaining row indexes (original numbering) in order.
practice.hint: Stop when no row is dominated.

practice.title: Social welfare
practice.intro: Write welfare(game, r, c): the sum of both players' payoffs in cell (r, c). Then return the pair [best cell sum over the whole game, sum at cell (r, c)].
practice.hint: Search all cells for the best total.

chapters.title: Mixed strategies and zero-sum games

maps.title: Mixed strategies
links: Value of game | is | Guaranteed payoff

summary: In matching pennies there is no pure equilibrium: whichever side you pick, the opponent wants to switch. The solution is to randomise, a mixed strategy, so the opponent cannot exploit a pattern.
In a mixed equilibrium each player chooses probabilities that make the other player indifferent between their strategies. For a 2x2 game this gives a simple formula.

In a zero-sum game, von Neumann's minimax theorem says the maximin value (the best guaranteed payoff) equals the minimax value (what the opponent can hold you to). This common number is the value of the game.

glossary.def: A probability distribution over pure strategies.
In a mixed equilibrium each player's mixing makes the other indifferent among the strategies they use.
The strategy that maximises the worst-case payoff.
The payoff both players can guarantee in a zero-sum game under optimal play.
A cell that is the minimum in its row and maximum in its column, giving a pure solution.

keyPoints: 2x2 mixing: choose p to make the opponent indifferent.
Matching pennies: 50-50.
Zero-sum: maximin = minimax.
Saddle point: pure equilibrium exists.
Mixed Nash always exists in finite games.

items: ELI5. In rock paper scissors, if you always pick rock you lose. The safest thing is to be a little bit random so nobody can guess you.

In rock paper scissors, any pattern gets punished. If you always choose rock, your opponent chooses paper. The only unexploitable play is to mix evenly. The probabilities are chosen not to make you win, but to leave the opponent with no better reply than any other.
Here is the indifference idea in a 2 by 2 game. Suppose the column player plays the first column with probability q. The row player's expected payoffs from the two rows are linear in q.

Choosing q so that those two are equal makes the row player indifferent, and then the row player can randomise in any way without loss. The row player's mixing is found by the same trick on the other side.

Mixed strategies can be seen as real randomisation, as in penalty kicks and poker bluffs, or as uncertainty about what the other will do. Studies of penalty kicks in football show that professionals mix almost exactly as the theory predicts, since a predictable kicker is a lost kicker.
Zero-sum games have a lovely extra property. One player wants to maximise, the other to minimise.

If I choose to guarantee my best worst-case, called maximin, and you choose to hold me to the lowest, called minimax, von Neumann proved in 1928 that the two numbers agree when mixed strategies are allowed. That number is the value of the game.

If a cell is both the smallest in its row and the largest in its column, it is a saddle point and the game is solved with pure strategies. Otherwise the solution mixes, and for bigger games it is found by linear programming, one of the great practical algorithms.

quiz.q: Why mix strategies?
What does the indifference principle say?
options: Mix so the opponent is indifferent

quiz.q: What is the value of a zero-sum game?
options: The guaranteed payoff under optimal play

quiz.q: Who proved the minimax theorem?
Matching pennies has what equilibrium?
What is a saddle point?
options: Min of its row and max of its column

practice.title: Match the term
practice.intro: Pair each term with its meaning.
pairs: pure solution of a zero-sum game

practice.title: Matching pennies mix
practice.intro: For a zero-sum 2x2 game with row payoffs [[a, b], [c, d]], the row player's probability of the first row that makes the column player indifferent is p = (d - c) / (a - b - c + d). Write mix_row(a, b, c, d), rounded to 4 decimals (assume the denominator is not zero).
practice.hint: Solve p a + (1-p) c = p b + (1-p) d.
practice.solution:
def mix_row(a, b, c, d):
    return round((d - c) / float(a - b - c + d), 4)

practice.title: Value of 2x2 game
practice.intro: Write game_value(a, b, c, d): the value of the zero-sum game with row payoffs [[a, b], [c, d]] when there is no saddle point: (a d - b c) / (a - b - c + d), rounded to 4 decimals.
practice.hint: Use the standard formula.
practice.solution:
def game_value(a, b, c, d):
    return round((a * d - b * c) / float(a - b - c + d), 4)

practice.title: Maximin and minimax
practice.intro: Write maximin_minimax(M): for a zero-sum game with row player's payoff matrix M (list of rows), return the list [maximin, minimax] using pure strategies only: the maximum over rows of the row minimum, and the minimum over columns of the column maximum.
practice.hint: Row minima then column maxima.

practice.title: Has a saddle point?
practice.intro: Write has_saddle(M): True if the pure maximin equals the pure minimax of the zero-sum matrix M, otherwise False.
practice.hint: They agree exactly when a saddle exists.

chapters.title: Classic games: dilemmas, coordination and conflict

maps.title: Classic games
links: Prisoner's dilemma | pits | Self against group
Battle of the sexes | needs | Coordination
Tragedy of the commons | overuses | Shared resource
Pareto optimal | means | No free improvement

summary: A handful of small games capture whole families of social situations. The prisoner's dilemma: defecting is dominant yet mutual cooperation is better for both. The stag hunt: two equilibria, one safe, one rewarding.
Chicken (or hawk-dove) rewards the one who does not swerve but ruins both if neither swerves. The battle of the sexes: two people prefer to be together but disagree on where.
The tension between individual incentive and group benefit appears in arms races, climate, overfishing, vaccination and team projects.

glossary.def: A game where defection is a dominant strategy but mutual cooperation gives both a better payoff.
A coordination game with a risky high-payoff equilibrium and a safe low-payoff one.
An anti-coordination game where each prefers to go straight if the other swerves.
An outcome where no player can be made better off without making another worse off.
Overuse of a shared resource because each user bears only a share of the cost.

keyPoints: PD: T > R > P > S.
Stag hunt: trust gives R, safe gives P.
Chicken: two asymmetric equilibria.
Coordination games: several equilibria.
Nash does not imply Pareto optimal.

items: ELI5. Two friends can each take all the sweets or share. Taking all is tempting, but if both do, they get less than if both share. That puzzle is called the prisoner's dilemma.

Two suspects are held apart. Each can stay silent or betray the other. If both stay silent, they each get a short sentence. If one betrays, the betrayer goes free and the other gets a long sentence. If both betray, both get a medium sentence. Whatever the other does, betraying is better for me.
So both betray, and both end up worse than if they had stayed silent. That is the prisoner's dilemma.

The numbers have a standard ordering. Temptation to defect T beats reward for mutual cooperation R, which beats punishment for mutual defection P, which beats the sucker's payoff S. With T above R above P above S, defection dominates.
Many real problems share this shape: arms races, price wars, polluting, doping in sport, and overfishing.

The stag hunt changes the incentives. Two hunters can hunt a stag together, which pays well, or each hunt a hare alone, which pays modestly but surely. Both stag and both hare are equilibria. The question is trust: if I doubt you, I take the hare.
Many cooperation problems are stag hunts rather than dilemmas, and fix themselves with communication and reputation.

Chicken is the game of two cars driving at each other. Going straight while the other swerves is best, swerving while the other goes straight is bad but survivable, and neither swerving is a catastrophe.
The equilibria are the two asymmetric ones, and each side tries to look committed, by throwing away the steering wheel, for example. Brinkmanship has this structure.

In the battle of the sexes, a couple wants to spend the evening together but one prefers the opera and the other the football. Both would rather go together to either than apart. This is a pure coordination game with two good equilibria and a fight about which.
Conventions such as driving on the right solve this on a large scale.

quiz.q: In the prisoner's dilemma, what is dominant?
What is the PD payoff ordering?
How many pure equilibria does the stag hunt have?
What does Chicken reward?
options: Not swerving when the other does

quiz.q: What is the tragedy of the commons?
Is the PD equilibrium Pareto optimal?

practice.title: Match the game
practice.intro: Pair each game with its feature.
pairs: do not swerve if the other does

practice.title: Is it a prisoner's dilemma?
practice.intro: Write is_pd(T, R, P, S): True if T > R > P > S and 2R > T + S, otherwise False.
practice.hint: Check all the inequalities.
practice.solution:
def is_pd(T, R, P, S):
    return T > R and R > P and P > S and 2 * R > T + S

practice.title: Build the PD
practice.intro: Write make_pd(T, R, P, S): the symmetric game as a list of rows of [row, col] pairs, with strategies ordered cooperate, defect: [[[R, R], [S, T]], [[T, S], [P, P]]].
practice.hint: Fill the matrix carefully.
practice.solution:
def make_pd(T, R, P, S):
    return [[[R, R], [S, T]], [[T, S], [P, P]]]

practice.title: Classify a 2x2 symmetric game
practice.intro: For a symmetric 2x2 game with row payoffs a (both play first), b (I play first, other second), c (I play second, other first), d (both play second) write classify(a, b, c, d): return 'dilemma' if c > a and d > b (second strategy dominant) and a > d; 'coordination' if a > c and d > b; 'chicken' if c > a and b > d; otherwise 'other'.
practice.hint: Check the three patterns in order.

practice.title: Common pool
practice.intro: Each of n players chooses to harvest h units; the pool yields total harvest T = n x h and each unit sells for max(0, 10 - T). Write profit(n, h): one player's profit h x max(0, 10 - n x h).
practice.hint: More harvest by everyone lowers the price.
practice.solution:
def profit(n, h):
    return h * max(0, 10 - n * h)

chapters.title: Sequential games and backward induction

maps.title: Sequential games
links: Extensive form | is | A game tree
Backward induction | solves | From the end
Subgame perfect | rules out | Empty threats

summary: When players move in turn and see earlier moves, the game is drawn as a tree. Backward induction solves it by starting at the last decisions and working back to the root.
A subgame perfect equilibrium is a Nash equilibrium that is also an equilibrium in every subgame. It rules out empty threats, plans nobody would carry out when the time came.
Moving first can be an advantage when it commits you, as in Stackelberg competition, but can be a disadvantage when it reveals information.

glossary.def: A game represented as a tree of decisions in order, with payoffs at the leaves.
Solving a finite sequential game by reasoning from the last move to the first.
A strategy profile that is a Nash equilibrium in every subgame.
A threat that would not be in the threatener's interest to carry out.
Limiting your own future options in order to change others' behaviour.

keyPoints: Solve from the leaves upward.
At each node, the mover picks the best payoff for themselves.
Subgame perfect = backward induction in finite perfect-information games.
Commitment can create value.
Ultimatum game: theory vs people.

items: ELI5. In chess you think backwards: if I do this, you do that, then I do this. Starting from the end and working back helps you choose the first move.

Chess is a sequential game: each player sees the board before moving. We draw such a game as a tree. Each node belongs to one player, each branch is a move, and each leaf shows the payoffs. To solve it, imagine yourself at the last decision. The mover there simply takes the best option.
Replace that node by its outcome, and move one step up.

This is backward induction. At each step, the player on move picks the branch giving them the highest payoff, given the already-solved continuations. When you reach the root you know the whole path. In a finite game with perfect information, this gives a clear prediction.
It also shows that chess has a best result under perfect play, though it is too large to compute.

Consider an entrant deciding whether to enter a market with a monopolist. The monopolist threatens a price war if the entrant enters. But if the entrant does enter, a price war hurts the monopolist too, so it would rather accommodate. The threat is empty.
Backward induction predicts entry and accommodation, a subgame perfect equilibrium. Threats must be credible to count.

Because commitment can make a threat credible, giving up options can be powerful. A general who burns the bridges behind the army shows there is no retreat. A company that builds extra capacity makes a price war credible.
In Stackelberg competition, the firm that moves first and commits to a large output forces the follower to adjust, and earns more than in the simultaneous game.

The ultimatum game tests the theory. One person proposes how to split ten pounds, and the other accepts or rejects, in which case both get nothing. Theory says offer the smallest amount and the other accepts.
In experiments people often offer nearly half and reject offers under about thirty percent. Fairness and emotion are part of the payoffs.

What is an empty threat?

options: Offer near half and reject low offers

practice.intro: A tree is either a leaf [payoff_player0, payoff_player1] (a list of two numbers) or a node ['player', child1, child2, ...] where player is 0 or 1. practice.title: Entry game
practice.intro: An entrant chooses In or Out. If Out, payoffs (0, 4) (entrant, incumbent). If In, the incumbent chooses Fight (payoffs -1, -1) or Accommodate (payoffs 2, 2). Write entry(fight_payoff_inc, accommodate_payoff_inc): by backward induction return 'in' if the entrant enters and 'out' if not, where the entrant gets -1 after Fight and 2 after Accommodate, and the incumbent's payoffs are the arguments.

practice.title: Stackelberg leader
practice.intro: Two firms with demand price = 100 - (q1 + q2), zero cost. The follower best-responds q2 = (100 - q1) / 2. Write leader_profit(q1): the leader's profit q1 x (100 - q1 - q2), rounded to 2 decimals.
practice.hint: Plug the follower's reply into the leader's profit.

practice.title: Ultimatum acceptance
practice.intro: Write ultimatum(offer, total, threshold): the responder accepts when offer / total >= threshold. Return the list [accepted (True/False), proposer's share] where the proposer's share is total - offer if accepted, otherwise 0.
practice.hint: A rejection leaves nothing.

chapters.title: Repeated games and the evolution of cooperation

maps.title: Repeated games
links: Shadow of the future | encourages | Cooperation
Tit for tat | copies | Last move

summary: If the prisoner's dilemma is played once, defection wins. If it is played repeatedly with no known end, the future can discipline the present: cooperating may be worth it to keep the other cooperating.

Robert Axelrod's tournaments found that a simple strategy, tit for tat (cooperate first, then copy the opponent's last move), outscored far more elaborate ones. It is nice, retaliatory, forgiving and clear.
The folk theorem says that when players value the future enough, almost any feasible outcome better than the minimum can be sustained as an equilibrium of the repeated game.

glossary.def: A game in which the same stage game is played many times.
Cooperate on the first round, then do whatever the opponent did last round.
Cooperate until the opponent defects once, then defect forever.
The weight delta between 0 and 1 on payoffs one round later.
In infinitely repeated games with patient players, many outcomes can be sustained in equilibrium.

keyPoints: Grim trigger sustains cooperation if delta >= (T - R) / (T - P).
Sum of delta^t = 1 / (1 - delta).
Last-round unravelling: known end means defect.
Tit for tat: nice, retaliating, forgiving, clear.
Reputation and repeat business support cooperation.

items: ELI5. If you play with the same friends every day, being nice pays off, because they will remember. Copying what they did last time is a good rule.

Shopkeepers who sell to the same neighbours every day tend to be honest. A one-time tourist trap can cheat. The difference is the future. In a repeated game, a player who defects today may lose cooperation tomorrow. The shadow of the future turns a dilemma into a problem that can be solved.

Grim trigger is a simple example: cooperate until the other defects once, then defect forever. Is cooperation worth it? Cooperating forever pays R each round, worth R over one minus delta in total, where delta is how much you value tomorrow compared with today.
Defecting pays T once and then P forever. Cooperation wins when delta is at least T minus R over T minus P.

If the number of rounds is known, the logic unravels. On the last round, defection is dominant. So on the second-to-last, the future gives no reward for cooperating, and so on back to the first round.
In practice people do cooperate in finite games, and uncertainty about the end or about the opponent's type restores cooperation.

In the 1980s, Robert Axelrod invited experts to submit programs for a computer tournament of the repeated prisoner's dilemma. The winner was the shortest, tit for tat, submitted by Anatol Rapoport. It starts by cooperating and then copies the opponent's previous move.
Axelrod noted that successful strategies were nice, never defecting first, yet retaliatory, forgiving and clear.

The folk theorem is the general result. When players are patient enough, any outcome that gives each player more than their worst-case payoff can be an equilibrium of the repeated game. Cooperation is possible, but so are many other outcomes.
Which one emerges depends on norms, history and institutions. The lab lets you run a tournament of strategies yourself.

practice.intro: Play a round-robin tournament of the repeated prisoner's dilemma between classic strategies and one you control by choosing a rule. Run the tournament with at least four strategies and see who wins.
practice.html: Payoffs: both cooperate 3 each, both defect 1 each, defector 5 vs cooperator 0. 50 rounds per match.

practice.title: Match the strategy
practice.intro: Pair each strategy with its behaviour.

practice.title: Tit for tat match
practice.intro: Write tft_vs(opp_moves): given the list of opponent moves ('C' or 'D'), return tit for tat's own moves: 'C' first, then the opponent's previous move each round (same length as opp_moves).
practice.hint: Look at the previous opponent move.

practice.title: Score a match
practice.intro: Write score(a_moves, b_moves, T, R, P, S): the total payoff of player A over the rounds, where each pair of moves earns R for CC, S for A=C vs B=D, T for A=D vs B=C, and P for DD. Return A's total as an integer.
practice.hint: Add the right payoff for each round.

practice.title: Discounted value
practice.intro: Write discounted(payoff, delta, rounds): the sum of payoff x delta^t for t = 0 to rounds-1, rounded to 4 decimals.
practice.hint: Weight round t by delta to the t.

practice.title: Minimum patience
practice.intro: Write min_delta(T, R, P): the smallest discount factor for which grim trigger sustains cooperation, (T - R) / (T - P), rounded to 4 decimals.
practice.hint: Compare cooperating forever with defecting once.
practice.solution:
def min_delta(T, R, P):
    return round((T - R) / float(T - P), 4)

chapters.title: Evolutionary game theory
summary: Evolutionary game theory replaces rational thought by selection: strategies that earn more payoff spread in the population, those that earn less shrink. No one needs to be clever.
An evolutionarily stable strategy (ESS) is one that, once common, cannot be invaded by a small group using a different strategy. Every strict Nash equilibrium is an ESS.
Replicator dynamics describe how the share of each strategy changes: x' = x (f - average fitness). In hawk-dove the population settles at a mix of hawks and doves.

glossary.def: A strategy that, if adopted by most of a population, cannot be displaced by a rare mutant.
Equations in which a strategy's share grows when its payoff is above the population average.
A contest over a resource in which hawks fight and doves share or retreat.
The payoff a strategy earns against the current population, interpreted as reproductive success.
A strategy's success depends on how common each strategy is.

keyPoints: x' = x (f(x) - average).
Hawk-dove ESS: share of hawks = V / C when C > V.
ESS: resists a small invasion.
Stable fixed point of the dynamics.
Payoffs become offspring.

items: ELI5. Animals do not think about games, but the ones whose habits work well have more babies, so good habits spread.

Biologists noticed that animals seldom fight to the death over territory, even though fighting is natural. John Maynard Smith and George Price explained this in 1973 with game theory. Evolution is a game where strategies are inherited and payoffs are offspring.

In the hawk-dove game, hawks always escalate and doves display and retreat. The resource is worth V. A fight costs C to the loser, sharing the cost. Two doves split V. A hawk beats a dove and takes all. Two hawks fight, getting V minus C over two each on average.
If C exceeds V, hawks can't take over: a population of all hawks is invaded by doves, and all doves is invaded by hawks.

The balance is a mixed equilibrium in which a fraction V over C of the population are hawks. At that mix, hawks and doves earn the same. Any drift toward more hawks makes hawks do worse, and the population returns. This fixed point is an evolutionarily stable state.

The replicator equation formalises this. The growth rate of strategy i's share is its share times the amount by which its fitness exceeds the average. Strategies above the average spread. Fixed points are where all present strategies earn the same.
The same maths describes the spread of ideas, habits and behaviours in cultures, where success is copied.

Evolutionary game theory explains the persistence of altruism, signalling and conventions. It also reveals that cooperation in the prisoner's dilemma dies out in a well-mixed population but can survive when like meets like, through kinship, reputation or local neighbourhoods.
The lab shows the dynamics for several games.

practice.intro: For a two-strategy population with share x of strategy 1, matrix A (payoffs [[a, b], [c, d]]) and a time step dt, write replicator(x, A, dt): f1 = a x + b (1-x), f2 = c x + d (1-x), average = x f1 + (1-x) f2, new x = x + dt x (f1 - average). Round to 4 decimals.

chapters.title: Auctions, bargaining and mechanism design

maps.title: Mechanism design
links: Incentive compatible | means | Truth is best

summary: Auctions are games with money. In a sealed-bid second-price (Vickrey) auction the highest bidder wins but pays the second-highest bid, and bidding your true value is a dominant strategy.

In a first-price auction you pay what you bid, so you shade your bid below your value. Under standard assumptions both formats give the seller the same expected revenue, the revenue equivalence theorem.
Mechanism design runs game theory backward: choose the rules so that selfish play produces the outcome you want. Vickrey, Clarke and Groves showed how truthful reporting can be made optimal.

glossary.def: A sealed-bid auction in which the highest bidder wins and pays the second-highest bid.
Bidding less than your true value in a first-price auction.
In common-value auctions the winner tends to have overestimated the value.
Designing rules of a game so that self-interested behaviour achieves a desired goal.
The split that maximises the product of the players' gains over their disagreement payoffs.

keyPoints: Vickrey: bid your value.
First price, 2 bidders uniform: bid v / 2.
Revenue equivalence: same expected revenue.
Nash bargaining: maximise (u1 - d1)(u2 - d2).
Incentive compatible: truth-telling is optimal.

items: ELI5. In an auction, the best way to be honest is to pay the price of the second-best bidder, so there is nothing to gain from fibbing.

Auctions price art, spectrum licences, oil fields and the ads you see online. They are games where the rules decide who wins and what is paid. The sealed-bid second-price auction has a lovely property.
The winner pays the second-highest bid, so your own bid only decides whether you win, not what you pay. Therefore bid your true value.

Why is truth best? If you bid higher than your value you may win at a price above your value and lose money. If you bid lower you may lose an auction you'd have profited from. Bidding exactly your value is never worse and sometimes better, so it is a dominant strategy.
Search engines use a variation of this to sell ad slots.

In a first-price auction the winner pays their own bid, so honest bidding earns zero profit. You bid below your value, trading a lower chance of winning against a higher profit if you win. With two bidders whose values are uniform between zero and one, the optimal bid is half your value.
Surprisingly, the seller's expected revenue is the same as in the Vickrey auction.

When the item has the same value to everyone but each bidder has only a noisy estimate, the winner is the one with the most optimistic estimate and likely overpaid. This is the winner's curse. Wise bidders shade their bids to correct for it. Oil companies learned this the hard way.
Mechanism design asks: what rules make people reveal what we need to know? Besides auctions, it covers matching students to schools, kidneys to patients and the design of voting rules.

Bargaining theory covers the two-person case: Nash's solution splits the surplus to maximise the product of gains, and Rubinstein's alternating offers model shows that patience gives bargaining power.

chapters.title: Cooperative games and social choice

maps.title: Cooperative games
links: Coalition | is | A group of players

summary: Cooperative game theory asks how a group that can bind its members should split the gains. A characteristic function says what each coalition can achieve alone.

The Shapley value gives each player their average marginal contribution over all orders in which the coalition could form. It is the unique allocation satisfying fairness axioms. The core is the set of allocations no coalition could improve on by leaving.

Social choice asks how to combine individual rankings into a group decision. Condorcet's paradox shows majorities can cycle, and Arrow's impossibility theorem shows that no ranking method satisfies a short list of fairness conditions.

glossary.def: A subset of players who agree to act together.
A function v(S) giving the value a coalition S can secure.
A player's average marginal contribution across all orders of joining the coalition.
The allocations that no coalition can improve upon by breaking away.
A situation where majority preferences form a cycle: A beats B, B beats C, C beats A.

keyPoints: phi_i = average of v(S + i) - v(S) over orders.
Efficient: Shapley values add to v(all).
Core: no coalition gets less than v(S).
Condorcet winner beats every other option.
Arrow: no perfect ranking rule.

items: ELI5. When a group wins together, who deserves how much? You can imagine people joining one at a time and give each what they add. Voting can go in circles too.
Three friends each bring something to a business. One has money, one skill and one a customer list. Alone, none can earn much, but together they earn a lot.
How should the profit be split? The characteristic function lists what every possible group, called a coalition, can earn, and the question is what each member deserves.

Lloyd Shapley's answer is to imagine the group forming one member at a time, in random order, and to pay each member what they add to the groups already there, their marginal contribution. Averaging over all orders gives the Shapley value.

It adds up to the total, treats equal players equally, and gives nothing to someone who adds nothing. It is used to explain machine learning predictions and to share costs among airlines using one runway.

The core takes a different view: an allocation is stable if no subgroup could do better by leaving. Some games have a core, others have none, and in some it contains many allocations. The Shapley value is always defined and is sometimes outside the core.

Voting is social choice. Suppose three voters rank candidates A, B and C as A over B over C, B over C over A, and C over A over B. A majority prefers A to B, a majority prefers B to C, and a majority prefers C to A. The majority preference runs in a circle.
This is the Condorcet paradox, found in 1785.
Kenneth Arrow proved in 1951 that no voting method that ranks three or more options can satisfy a short list of reasonable conditions: unanimity, independence of irrelevant options, and no dictator.
Gibbard and Satterthwaite later showed that any reasonable method can be manipulated by insincere voting. Every voting system has trade-offs, and choosing one means choosing which flaws to accept.

practice.title: Shapley value for 3 players
practice.intro: Write shapley(v): v is a dict-free list of 8 values giving the worth of coalitions indexed by bitmask (bit 0 = player 0, bit 1 = player 1, bit 2 = player 2), so v[0] = 0 and v[7] is the grand coalition. Return the list of Shapley values for players 0, 1, 2 (averaging over all 6 orders), rounded to 3 decimals.
practice.hint: Add each player's marginal contribution in every order.

practice.title: Efficiency check
practice.intro: Write efficient(v, alloc): True if the allocation list alloc adds up to v[7], the grand coalition's worth (compare with a tolerance of 0.001).
practice.hint: Sum the allocation.
practice.solution:
def efficient(v, alloc):
    return abs(sum(alloc) - v[7]) < 0.001

practice.title: In the core?
practice.intro: Write in_core(v, alloc): True if for every coalition mask from 1 to 7 the sum of alloc over its members is at least v[mask], and the total equals v[7] (tolerance 0.001).
practice.hint: Test each of the seven coalitions.

practice.title: Pairwise majority
practice.intro: Write majority(ballots, a, b): ballots is a list of rankings (each a list of candidate names, best first). Return the candidate preferred by more voters, between a and b, or 'tie' if equal.
practice.hint: Count which comes earlier on each ballot.
